Eigenvalue problems

“Eigenvalue” means characteristic value. These types of problems show up in many areas involving boundary-value problems, where we may not be able to obtain an analytical solution, but we can identify certain characteristic values that tell us important information about the system: the eigenvalues.

# import libraries for numerical functions and plotting
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
# these lines are only for helping improve the display
import matplotlib_inline.backend_inline
matplotlib_inline.backend_inline.set_matplotlib_formats('pdf', 'png')
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi']= 300
plt.rcParams['savefig.dpi'] = 300

Example: beam buckling¶

Let’s consider deflection in a simply supported (static) vertical beam: y(x)y(x)y(x), with boundary conditions y(0)=0y(0) = 0y(0)=0 and y(L)=0y(L) = 0y(L)=0. To get the governing equation, start with considering the sum of moments around the upper pin:

∑M=Mz+Py=0Mz=−Py\begin{align} \sum M &= M_z + P y = 0 \\ M_z &= -P y \end{align}∑MMz​​=Mz​+Py=0=−Py​​
(1)

We also know that Mz=EIy′′M_z = E I y''Mz​=EIy′′, so we can obtain

Mz=EId2ydx2=−Pyy′′+PEIy=0\begin{align} M_z = E I \frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} &= -P y \\ y'' + \frac{P}{EI} y &= 0 \end{align}Mz​=EIdx2d2y​y′′+EIP​y​=−Py=0​​
(2)

This equation governs the stability of a beam, considering small deflections. To simplify things, let’s define λ2=PEI\lambda^2 = \frac{P}{EI}λ2=EIP​, which gives us the ODE

y′′+λ2y=0y'' + \lambda^2 y = 0y′′+λ2y=0
(3)

We can get the general solution to this:

y(x)=Acos⁡(λx)+Bsin⁡(λx)y(x) = A \cos (\lambda x) + B \sin (\lambda x)y(x)=Acos(λx)+Bsin(λx)
(4)

To find the coefficients, let’s apply the boundary conditions, starting with x=0x=0x=0:

y(x=0)=0=Acos⁡0+Bsin⁡0→A=0y(x=L)=0=Bsin⁡(λL)\begin{align} y(x=0) &= 0 = A \cos 0 + B \sin 0 \\ \rightarrow A &= 0 \\ y(x=L) &= 0 = B \sin (\lambda L) \end{align}y(x=0)→Ay(x=L)​=0=Acos0+Bsin0=0=0=Bsin(λL)​​
(5)

Now what? B≠0B \neq 0B=0, because otherwise we would have the trivial solution y(x)=0y(x) = 0y(x)=0. Instead, to satisfy the boundary condition, we need

B≠0→sin⁡(λL)=0soλL=nπn=1,2,3,…,∞λ=nπLn=1,2,3,…,∞\begin{align} B \neq 0 \rightarrow \sin (\lambda L) &= 0 \\ \text{so} \quad \lambda L &= n \pi \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, \infty \\ \lambda &= \frac{n \pi}{L} \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, \infty \end{align}B=0→sin(λL)soλLλ​=0=nπn=1,2,3,…,∞=Lnπ​n=1,2,3,…,∞​​
(6)

λ\lambdaλ give the the eigenvalues for this problem; as you can see, there are an infinite number, that correspond to eigenfunctions:

yn=Bsin⁡(nπxL)n=1,2,3,…,∞y_n = B \sin \left( \frac{n \pi x}{L} \right) \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, \inftyyn​=Bsin(Lnπx​)n=1,2,3,…,∞
(7)

The eigenvalues and associated eigenfunctions physically represent different modes of deflection. For example, consider the first three modes (corresponding to n=1,2,3n = 1, 2, 3n=1,2,3):

L = 1.0

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3)

x = np.linspace(0, L)
y = np.sin(np.pi * x / L)
axes[0].plot(y, x)
axes[0].set_title('n = 1')

y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x / L)
axes[1].plot(y, x)
axes[1].set_title('n = 2')

y = np.sin(3 * np.pi * x / L)
axes[2].plot(y, x)
axes[2].set_title('n = 3')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Loading...

Here we see different modes of how the beam will buckle. How do we know when this happens?

Recall that the eigenvalue is connected to the physical properties of the beam:

λ2=PEI→λ=PEI=nπLP=EILn2π2\begin{gather} \lambda^2 = \frac{P}{EI} \rightarrow \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{P}{EI}} = \frac{n \pi}{L} \\ P = \frac{EI}{L} n^2 \pi^2 \end{gather}λ2=EIP​→λ=EIP​​=Lnπ​P=LEI​n2π2​​
(8)

This means that when the combination of load force and beam properties match certain values, the beam will deflect—and buckle—in one of the modes corresponding to the associated eigenfunction.

In particular, the first mode (n=1n=1n=1) is interesting, because this is the first one that will be encountered if a load starts at zero and increases. This is the Euler critical load of buckling, PcrP_{cr}Pcr​:

λ1=πL→λ12=PEI=π2L2Pcr=π2EIL2\begin{gather} \lambda_1 = \frac{\pi}{L} \rightarrow \lambda_1^2 = \frac{P}{EI} = \frac{\pi^2}{L^2} \\ P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{L^2} \end{gather}λ1​=Lπ​→λ12​=EIP​=L2π2​Pcr​=L2π2EI​​​
(9)

Example: beam buckling with different boundary conditions¶

Let’s consider a slightly different case, where at x=0x=0x=0 the beam is supported such that y′(0)=0y'(0) = 0y′(0)=0. How does the beam buckle in this case?

The governing equation and general solution are the same:

y′′+λ2y=0y(x)=Acos⁡(λx)+Bsin⁡(λx)\begin{align} y'' + \lambda^2 y &= 0 \\ y(x) &= A \cos (\lambda x) + B \sin (\lambda x) \end{align}y′′+λ2yy(x)​=0=Acos(λx)+Bsin(λx)​​
(10)

but our boundary conditions are now different:

y′(0)=0=−λAsin⁡(0)+λBcos⁡(0)→B=0y=Acos⁡(λx)y(L)=0=Acos⁡(λL)A≠0→cos⁡(λL)=0soλL=(2n−1)π2n=1,2,3,…,∞λ=(2n−1)π2Ln=1,2,3,…,∞\begin{align} y'(0) = 0 = -\lambda A \sin(0) + \lambda B\cos(0) \\ \rightarrow B &= 0 \\ y &= A \cos (\lambda x) \\ y(L) &= 0 = A \cos (\lambda L) \\ A \neq 0 \rightarrow \cos(\lambda L) &= 0 \\ \text{so} \quad \lambda L &= \frac{(2n-1) \pi}{2} \quad n = 1,2,3,\ldots, \infty \\ \lambda &= \frac{(2n-1) \pi}{2 L} \quad n = 1,2,3,\ldots, \infty \end{align}y′(0)=0=−λAsin(0)+λBcos(0)→Byy(L)A=0→cos(λL)soλLλ​=0=Acos(λx)=0=Acos(λL)=0=2(2n−1)π​n=1,2,3,…,∞=2L(2n−1)π​n=1,2,3,…,∞​​
(11)

Then, the critical buckling load, again corresponding to n=1n=1n=1, is

Pcr=π2EI4L2P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{4 L^2}Pcr​=4L2π2EI​
(12)

Getting eigenvalues numerically¶

We can only get the eigenvalues analytically if we can obtain an analytical solution of the ODE, but we might want to get eigenvalues for more complex problems too. In that case, we can use an approach based on finite differences to find the eigenvalues.

Consider the same problem as above, for deflection of a simply supported beam:

y′′+λ2y=0y'' + \lambda^2 y = 0y′′+λ2y=0
(13)

with boundary conditions y(0)=0y(0) = 0y(0)=0 and y(L)=0y(L) = 0y(L)=0. Let’s represent this using finite differences, for a case where L=3L=3L=3 and Δx=1\Delta x = 1Δx=1, so we have four points in our solution grid.

The finite difference representation of the ODE is:

yi−1−2yi+yi+1Δx2+λ2yi=0yi−1+(λ2Δx2−2)yi+yi+1=0\begin{align} \frac{y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}}{\Delta x^2} + \lambda^2 y_i &= 0 \\ y_{i-1} + \left( \lambda^2 \Delta x^2 - 2 \right) y_i + y_{i+1} &= 0 \end{align}Δx2yi−1​−2yi​+yi+1​​+λ2yi​yi−1​+(λ2Δx2−2)yi​+yi+1​​=0=0​​
(14)

However, in this case, we are not solving for the values of deflection (yiy_iyi​), but instead the eigenvalues λ\lambdaλ.

Then, we can write the system of equations using the above recursion formula and our two boundary conditions:

y1=0y1+y2(λ2Δx2−2)+y3=0y2+y3(λ2Δx2−2)+y4=0y4=0\begin{align} y_1 &= 0 \\ y_1 + y_2 \left( \lambda^2 \Delta x^2 - 2 \right) + y_3 &= 0 \\ y_2 + y_3 \left( \lambda^2 \Delta x^2 - 2 \right) + y_4 &= 0 \\ y_4 &= 0 \end{align}y1​y1​+y2​(λ2Δx2−2)+y3​y2​+y3​(λ2Δx2−2)+y4​y4​​=0=0=0=0​​
(15)

which we can simplify down to two equations by incorporating the boundary conditions into the equations for the two middle points, and also letting k=λ2Δx2k = \lambda^2 \Delta x^2k=λ2Δx2:

y2(k−2)+y3=0y2+y3(k−2)=0\begin{align} y_2 (k-2) + y_3 &= 0 \\ y_2 + y_3 (k-2) &= 0 \end{align}y2​(k−2)+y3​y2​+y3​(k−2)​=0=0​​
(16)

Let’s modify this once more by multiplying both equations by -1:

y2(2−k)−y3=0−y2+y3(2−k)=0\begin{align} y_2 (2-k) - y_3 &= 0 \\ -y_2 + y_3 (2-k) &= 0 \end{align}y2​(2−k)−y3​−y2​+y3​(2−k)​=0=0​​
(17)

Now we can represent this system of equations as a matrix equation Ay=b=0A \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}Ay=b=0:

[2−k−1−12−k][y2y3]=[00]\begin{bmatrix} 2-k & -1 \\ -1 & 2-k \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_2 \\ y_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[2−k−1​−12−k​][y2​y3​​]=[00​]
(18)

y=0\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}y=0 is a trivial solution to this, so instead det⁡(A)=0\det(A) = 0det(A)=0 satisfies this equation. For our 2×22\times 22×2 matrix, that looks like:

det⁡(A)=∣2−k−1−12−k∣=(2−k)2−1=0k2−4k+3=0(k−3)(k−1)=0\begin{align} \det(A) = \begin{vmatrix} 2-k & -1 \\ -1 & 2-k \end{vmatrix} = (2-k)^2 - 1 &= 0 \\ k^2 - 4k + 3 &= 0 \\ (k-3)(k-1) &= 0 \end{align}det(A)=∣∣​2−k−1​−12−k​∣∣​=(2−k)2−1k2−4k+3(k−3)(k−1)​=0=0=0​​
(19)

so the roots of this equation are k1=1k_1 = 1k1​=1 and k2=3k_2 = 3k2​=3. Recall that kkk is directly related to the eigenvalue: k=λ2Δx2k = \lambda^2 \Delta x^2k=λ2Δx2, and Δx=1\Delta x = 1Δx=1 for this case, so we can calculate the two associated eigenvalues:

k1=λ12Δx2=1→λ1=1k2=λ22Δx2=3→λ2=3=1.732\begin{align} k_1 &= \lambda_1^2 \Delta x^2 = 1 \rightarrow \lambda_1 = 1 \\ k_2 &= \lambda_2^2 \Delta x^2 = 3 \rightarrow \lambda_2 = \sqrt{3} = 1.732 \end{align}k1​k2​​=λ12​Δx2=1→λ1​=1=λ22​Δx2=3→λ2​=3​=1.732​​
(20)

Our work has given us approximations for the first two eigenvalues. We can compare these against the exact values, given in general by λ=nπ/L\lambda = n \pi / Lλ=nπ/L (which we determined above):

n=1:λ1=πL=π3=1.0472n=2:λ2=2πL=2π3=2.0944\begin{align} n=1: \quad \lambda_1 &= \frac{\pi}{L} = \frac{\pi}{3} = 1.0472 \\ n=2: \quad \lambda_2 &= \frac{2\pi}{L} = \frac{2\pi}{3} = 2.0944 \end{align}n=1:λ1​n=2:λ2​​=Lπ​=3π​=1.0472=L2π​=32π​=2.0944​​
(21)

So, our approximations are close, but with some obvious error. This is because we used a fairly crude step size of Δx=1\Delta x = 1Δx=1, dividing the domain into just three segments. By using a finer resolution, we can get more-accurate eigenvalues and also more of them (remember, there are actually an infinite number!).

To do that, we will need to use Python, which offers the np.linalg.eigvals() function for calculating eigenvalues---essentially it is finding the roots to the polynomial given by det⁡(A)=0\det(A) = 0det(A)=0. We need to modify this slightly, though, to use the function:

det⁡(A)=0det⁡(A∗−kI)=0\begin{align} \det(A) &= 0 \\ \det \left( A^* - k I \right) = 0 \end{align}det(A)det(A∗−kI)=0​=0​
(22)

where the new matrix is

A∗=[2−1−12]A^* = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}A∗=[2−1​−12​]
(23)

Then, np.linalg.eigvals(A*) will provide the values of kkk, which we can use to find the λ\lambdaλs:

dx = 1.0
L = 3.0

Astar = np.array([[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
k = np.linalg.eigvals(Astar)

lambdas = np.sqrt(k) / dx

print(f'λ_1: {lambdas[0]: 5.3f}')
print(f'λ_2: {lambdas[1]: 5.3f}')
λ_1:  1.732
λ_2:  1.000

As expected, this matches with our manual calculation above. But, we might want to calculate these eigenvalues more accurately, so let’s generalize this a bit and then try using Δx=0.1\Delta x= 0.1Δx=0.1:

dx = 0.1
L = 3.0
x = np.arange(0, L+0.001, dx)

Astar = np.zeros((len(x)-2, len(x)-2))
Astar[0,0] = 2
Astar[0,1] = -1
Astar[-1,-2] = -1
Astar[-1,-1] = 2
for idx in range(len(Astar) - 1):
    if idx > 0 and idx < len(Astar) - 1:
        Astar[idx,idx-1] = -1
        Astar[idx,idx] = 2
        Astar[idx,idx+1] = -1

# sort in ascending order
k = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvals(Astar))

lambdas = np.sqrt(k) / dx

print(f'λ_1: {lambdas[0]: 5.3f}')
print(f'λ_2: {lambdas[1]: 5.3f}')

err = 100*np.abs(lambdas[0] - (np.pi/L)) / (np.pi/L)
print(f'Error in λ_1: {err: .2f}%')
λ_1:  1.047
λ_2:  2.091
Error in λ_1:  0.05%

Example: mass-spring system¶

Let’s analyze the motion of masses connected by springs in a system:

figure-md - Unknown Directive
<img src="../../images/mass-spring-system.jpg" alt="mass-spring system" class="bg-primary mb-1" width="400px">

System with two masses connected by springs

First, we need to write the equations of motion, based on doing a free-body diagram on each mass:

m1d2x1dt2=−kx1+k(x2−x1)m2d2x2dt2=−k(x2−x1)−kx2\begin{align} m_1 \frac{d^2 x_1}{dt^2} &= -k x_1 + k(x_2 - x_1) \\ m_2 \frac{d^2 x_2}{dt^2} &= -k (x_2 - x_1) - k x_2 \end{align}m1​dt2d2x1​​m2​dt2d2x2​​​=−kx1​+k(x2​−x1​)=−k(x2​−x1​)−kx2​​​
(24)

We can condense these equations a bit:

x1′′−km1(−2x1+x2)=0x2′′−km2(x1−2x2)=0\begin{align} x_1^{\prime\prime} - \frac{k}{m_1} \left( -2 x_1 + x_2 \right) &= 0 \\ x_2^{\prime\prime} - \frac{k}{m_2} \left( x_1 - 2 x_2 \right) &= 0 \end{align}x1′′​−m1​k​(−2x1​+x2​)x2′′​−m2​k​(x1​−2x2​)​=0=0​​
(25)

To proceed, we can assume that the masses will move in a sinusoidal fashion, with a shared frequency but separate amplitude:

xi=Aisin⁡(ωt)xi′′=−Aiω2sin⁡(ωt)\begin{align} x_i &= A_i \sin (\omega t) \\ x_i^{\prime\prime} &= -A_i \omega^2 \sin (\omega t) \end{align}xi​xi′′​​=Ai​sin(ωt)=−Ai​ω2sin(ωt)​​
(26)

We can plug these into the ODEs:

sin⁡(ωt)[(2km1−ω2)A1−km1A2]=0sin⁡(ωt)[−km2A1+(2km2−ω2)A2]=0\begin{align} \sin (\omega t) \left[ \left( \frac{2k}{m_1} - \omega^2 \right) A_1 - \frac{k}{m_1} A_2 \right] &= 0 \\ \sin (\omega t) \left[ -\frac{k}{m_2} A_1 + \left( \frac{2k}{m_2} - \omega^2 \right) A_2 \right] &= 0 \end{align}sin(ωt)[(m1​2k​−ω2)A1​−m1​k​A2​]sin(ωt)[−m2​k​A1​+(m2​2k​−ω2)A2​]​=0=0​​
(27)

or

(2km1−ω2)A1−km1A2=0−km2A1+(2km2−ω2)A2=0\begin{align} \left( \frac{2k}{m_1} - \omega^2 \right) A_1 - \frac{k}{m_1} A_2 &= 0 \\ -\frac{k}{m_2} A_1 + \left( \frac{2k}{m_2} - \omega^2 \right) A_2 &= 0 \end{align}(m1​2k​−ω2)A1​−m1​k​A2​−m2​k​A1​+(m2​2k​−ω2)A2​​=0=0​​
(28)

Let’s put some numbers in, and try to solve for the eigenvalues: ω2\omega^2ω2. Let m1=m2=40m_1 = m_2 = 40 m1​=m2​=40 kg and k=200k = 200k=200 N/m.

Now, the equations become

(10−ω2)A1−5A2=0−5A1+(10−ω2)A2=0\begin{align} \left( 10 - \omega^2 \right) A_1 - 5 A_2 &= 0 \\ -5 A_1 + \left( 10 - \omega^2 \right) A_2 &= 0 \end{align}(10−ω2)A1​−5A2​−5A1​+(10−ω2)A2​​=0=0​​
(29)

or Ay=0A \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}Ay=0, which we can represent as

[10−ω2−5−510−ω2][A1A2]=[00]\begin{bmatrix} 10-\omega^2 & -5 \\ -5 & 10-\omega^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} A_1 \\ A_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[10−ω2−5​−510−ω2​][A1​A2​​]=[00​]
(30)

Here, ω2\omega^2ω2 are the eigenvalues, and we can find them with det⁡(A)=0\det(A) = 0det(A)=0:

det⁡(B)=0det⁡(B∗−ω2I)=0\begin{align} \det(B) &= 0 \\ \det (B^* - \omega^2 I) &= 0 \end{align}det(B)det(B∗−ω2I)​=0=0​​
(31)
Bstar = np.array([[10, -5], [-5, 10]])
omega_squared = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvals(Bstar))
omega = np.sqrt(omega_squared)

print(f'ω_1 = {omega[0]: .2f} rad/s')
print(f'ω_2 = {omega[1]: .2f} rad/s')
ω_1 =  2.24 rad/s
ω_2 =  3.87 rad/s

We find there are two modes of oscillation, each associated with a different natural frequency. Unfortunately, we cannot calculate independent and unique values for the amplitudes, but if we insert the values of ω\omegaω into the above equations, we can find relations connecting the amplitudes:

ω1:A1=A2ω2:A1=−A2\begin{align} \omega_1: \quad A_1 &= A_2 \\ \omega_2: \quad A_1 &= -A_2 \end{align}ω1​:A1​ω2​:A1​​=A2​=−A2​​​
(32)

So, for the first mode, we have the two masses moving in sync with the same amplitude. In the second mode, they move with opposite (but equal) amplitude. With the two different frequencies, they also have two different periods:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5)

time = np.linspace(0, 3)
axes[0].plot(np.sin(omega[0]*time), time)
axes[0].plot(0, 0, 's')
axes[0].invert_yaxis()
axes[0].axis('off')

axes[1].plot(np.sin(omega[0]*time), time)
axes[1].plot(0, 0, 's')
axes[1].invert_yaxis()
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[1].text(-2.7,-0.2, 'First mode')

axes[2].axis('off')

axes[3].plot(-np.sin(omega[1]*time), time)
axes[3].plot(0, 0, 's')
axes[3].invert_yaxis()
axes[3].axis('off')
axes[3].text(0.4, -0.2, 'Second mode')

axes[4].plot(np.sin(omega[1]*time), time)
axes[4].plot(0, 0, 's')
axes[4].invert_yaxis()
axes[4].axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Loading...

We can confirm that the system would actually behave in this way by setting up the system of ODEs and integrating based on initial conditions matching the amplitudes of the two modes.

For example, let’s use x1(t=0)=x2(t=0)=1x_1 (t=0) = x_2(t=0) = 1x1​(t=0)=x2​(t=0)=1 for the first mode, and x1(t=0)=1x_1(t=0) = 1x1​(t=0)=1 and x2(t=0)=−1x_2(t=0) = -1x2​(t=0)=−1 for the second mode. We’ll use zero initial velocity for both cases.

Then, we can solve by converting the system of two 2nd-order ODEs into a system of four 1st-order ODEs:

def masses(t, x):
    '''calculates derivatives associated with the system'''
    m1 = 40
    m2 = 40
    k = 200
    
    return [
        x[1],
        (k/m1) * (-2*x[0] + x[2]),
        x[3],
        (k/m2) * (x[0] - 2*x[2]),
        ]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)

# integration for the system in the first mode
sol1 = solve_ivp(masses, [0, 3], [1, 0, 1, 0], max_step=0.1)

axes[0].plot(sol1.t, sol1.y[0,:])
axes[0].grid(True)
axes[0].set_ylabel('displacement (m)')
axes[0].set_title('First mode')
axes[1].plot(sol1.t, sol1.y[2,:])
axes[1].invert_yaxis()
axes[1].grid(True)
axes[1].set_xlabel('time (s)')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)

# integration for the system in second mode
sol2 = solve_ivp(masses, [0, 3], [1, 0, -1, 0], max_step=0.1)

axes[0].plot(sol2.t, sol2.y[0,:])
axes[0].grid(True)
axes[0].set_ylabel('displacement (m)')
axes[0].set_title('Second mode')
axes[1].plot(sol2.t, sol2.y[2,:])
axes[1].grid(True)
axes[1].set_xlabel('time (s)')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Loading...
Loading...

This shows that we get either of the pure modes of motion with the appropriate initial conditions.

What about if the initial conditions don’t match either set of amplitude patterns?

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)

# integration for the system in the first mode
sol1 = solve_ivp(masses, [0, 3], [0.25, 0, 0.75, 0], max_step=0.1)

axes[0].plot(sol1.t, sol1.y[0,:])
axes[0].grid(True)
axes[0].set_ylabel('displacement (m)')
axes[1].plot(sol1.t, sol1.y[2,:])
axes[1].invert_yaxis()
axes[1].grid(True)
axes[1].set_xlabel('time (s)')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
